title: Types of Political Systems
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the full spectrum of political systems -- from open democracies to total dictatorships -- and why the labels we use can mislead as much as they reveal.
competenceGoals: discuss and elaborate on political systems in English-speaking countries and compare with the Norwegian system
analyse how different political systems affect the rights and freedoms of individuals

content.content:
## Why the same word can mean very different things

Imagine two countries that both call themselves republics and both hold elections. In one, opposition parties campaign freely, newspapers criticise the leader on the front page, and an independent court can overrule the government. In the other, the only candidates are approved by the ruling party, journalists who ask hard questions disappear, and the courts do what they are told. Same labels -- republic, election -- but utterly different realities.

That gap is what this chapter is about. Not all countries are governed the same way, and political systems sit on a broad spectrum rather than in two neat boxes marked "good" and "bad." Learning to map that spectrum helps you appreciate freedoms you might take for granted, read global events more sharply, and think critically about how power is organised anywhere -- including in your own country.

## A spectrum from open to total control

Think of political systems as a sliding scale from the most open and participatory to the most restrictive and controlled. At the open end sits **liberal democracy**, where citizens enjoy broad political rights and civil liberties, and power is limited by a constitution, separated branches and free elections -- Norway, Canada, Germany and New Zealand are examples.

A step along, you find the **illiberal or flawed democracy**. Elections still happen, but civil liberties may be squeezed, opposition weakened, or media brought under control, so the country keeps a democratic shopfront while undermining democratic norms behind it. Hungary under Viktor Orban and Turkey have both drawn this criticism. Further along comes the **hybrid regime**, a genuine mix of democratic and authoritarian features where elections are held but are not fully free or fair, and some opposition is tolerated within tight limits.

Near the controlled end sits the **authoritarian regime**, where power is concentrated in a leader or ruling group with little public accountability, opposition and free media are suppressed, yet some personal freedoms may survive -- China under the Communist Party and Saudi Arabia are often cited. At the very end is the **totalitarian regime**, which seeks total control over political, economic, social and cultural life. A single party or leader holds absolute power, backed by an official ideology and pervasive propaganda, and independent organisations, free press and dissent are eliminated entirely. The historical examples are chilling: Nazi Germany under Hitler, the Soviet Union under Stalin, and North Korea today. Crucially, these are not rigid boxes. Many countries blend features of several types, and systems can shift over time -- towards democracy (*democratisation*) or away from it (*democratic backsliding*).

exercise.task: Test yourself on the spectrum of political systems:

questions.task: What most clearly distinguishes a totalitarian regime from an authoritarian one?

options.text: Totalitarian regimes hold no elections at all
Authoritarian regimes always have a single ruling ideology
Authoritarian regimes ban all personal freedoms
Totalitarian regimes seek total control over all aspects of life

questions.solution: Totalitarian regimes aim for complete control of political, economic, social and cultural life, usually backed by an official ideology. Authoritarian regimes concentrate political power but may leave some personal freedoms intact.

questions.task: A country holds elections but controls the media and weakens the opposition while keeping a democratic appearance. What is this best called?
questions.solution: An illiberal or flawed democracy maintains the outward form of democracy -- elections -- while undermining civil liberties and democratic norms.

options.text: A country becoming more democratic over time
A country moving away from democracy

questions.solution: Democratic backsliding is the process of a country moving away from democratic norms, the opposite of democratisation.

questions.task: Why does the chapter warn against treating these categories as rigid boxes?

options.text: Because all countries are actually identical
Because many countries blend features and can change over time
Because only totalitarian states really exist

questions.solution: Real countries often combine features of more than one type, and systems shift toward or away from democracy, so the categories are points on a spectrum rather than fixed boxes.

content.content:
## Monarchy or republic, federal or unitary -- and why the labels deceive

There is a second way to sort political systems: by how the head of state is chosen and how power is spread across territory. Start with the head of state. In an **absolute monarchy**, the monarch actually rules, often by decree -- rare today, with Saudi Arabia a leading example. In a **constitutional monarchy**, the monarch is a ceremonial head of state while elected officials wield real power; Norway, the United Kingdom, Sweden and Japan all fit here. In a **republic**, the head of state is elected, either directly by the people as in France and the USA, or by the legislature as in Germany and India. Here is the trap worth remembering: being a republic tells you nothing about how democratic a country is. A republic can be a thriving democracy or a brutal dictatorship -- the label describes the head of state, not the freedoms of citizens.

The second axis is geographic. In a **unitary system**, power is concentrated in the central government; regional and local bodies exist but draw their authority from the centre -- Norway, the UK and France work this way. In a **federal system**, power is constitutionally divided between a central government and regional units, each with its own areas of authority: the United States with its fifty states, Germany with sixteen Lander, Canada with its provinces, Australia. This matters in daily life. Federal systems can accommodate regional diversity and add another layer of checks on power, while unitary systems can deliver more uniform policy across the whole country. To see all of this in action, compare the UK and China: in the UK, power flows *upward* from citizens through elections to an accountable government; in China, power flows *downward* from the Communist Party leadership. That single difference in direction shapes almost everything else about life in the two states.

exercise.task: Test yourself on monarchies, republics and federal systems:

questions.task: Why does the text say that calling a country a "republic" tells you little about its democracy?

options.text: Because the term only describes how the head of state is chosen, not citizens' freedoms

questions.solution: "Republic" only means the head of state is elected rather than hereditary. A republic can be democratic or authoritarian, so the label says nothing about freedoms.

questions.task: What is the key feature of a federal system?

options.text: Power is constitutionally divided between central and regional governments
All power rests with the central government
The head of state is always a monarch

questions.solution: In a federal system, such as the US or Germany, power is constitutionally split between a central government and regional units that each have their own areas of authority.

questions.task: In a constitutional monarchy like Norway or the UK, the monarch is best described as:

options.text: The ruler who makes all major decisions
A ceremonial head of state while elected officials hold real power

questions.solution: In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is a ceremonial head of state; real political power lies with elected officials.

questions.task: The contrast between the UK and China is summed up as a difference in:

options.text: The direction in which power flows

questions.solution: In the UK power flows upward from citizens through elections; in China it flows downward from the party leadership -- a difference that shapes political life in each.

content.content:
## In short

Political systems form a spectrum, from open liberal democracies through flawed democracies and hybrid regimes to authoritarian and totalitarian states. Authoritarian regimes restrict political freedoms; totalitarian ones seek control over every part of life. A second set of labels describes how the head of state is chosen -- monarchy or republic -- and how power is spread across territory -- unitary or federal. But labels can mislead: a republic may be free or unfree, and the real test is how power is checked and where it ultimately flows. Above all, these systems are not frozen. Countries democratise and backslide, which is why reading any government carefully, rather than by its label, is a skill worth having.
